meta.note: Ubiquitous-language ontology for task-framework's domain: the vocabulary the code embodies, and the explicit typed relations between terms (is-a, part-of, relates, persists, references, describes). Deliberately separate from concept_store/concepts.json -- that store is architecture PER MODULE (one summary per file, enforced 1:1 by tests/test_concepts.py) and answers 'what does this module promise'. This file is vocabulary PER DOMAIN TERM and answers 'what is this thing, and what is it to the others' -- a term here can span several modules, and a module can define several terms, so it does not fit concept_store's per-file shape. Ground truth is still the code; this is a durable, human-readable map of the graph rather than N separate summaries.

bounded_contexts.Task Tracking: The core domain: tasks (some flagged as epics), their checklists, the links between tasks, and which task is currently active.
bounded_contexts.Loop Memory: Lessons the grooming/introspection loop produces that nothing else can hold -- separate vocabulary, separate lifecycle, only loosely coupled to Task Tracking by citation.
bounded_contexts.Architectural Knowledge: What each source module promises, tracked in concept_store/concepts.json -- describes the codebase itself, not tasks or memories.

Task.definition: One unit of work: id, epic flag, status, resolution (checklist), tags, notes, grooming findings, introspection reports. The single typed object the whole domain is built around. 'epic' is a plain boolean on this record (default False), not a subtype and not a term of its own -- a boolean carries everything the earlier two-value 'type' enum did, with no malformable value left to validate. Its sole effect is that an epic Task takes no parent; teams set it to mark a Task that others are grouped beneath, but that grouping is a convention, not a rule -- nothing requires a child's parent to be an epic. The parent/child hierarchy is a self-referential link from a Task to at most one parent Task, and no Task may be its own parent. A Task also carries a Scope naming the project it was created under, recorded at creation and never inferred afterwards.
Task.lifecycle: A Task is walked through four skills, each with one intention: task-create to open it, task-grooming to remove uncertainty before work starts, task-implementation to do the work, task-introspection to grade how well grooming predicted it and feed Loop Memory. None is mandatory, but skipping one leaves a Nudge behind.

TaskStatus.definition: The lifecycle state carried on a Task, drawn from a fixed, closed set of four values (open, blocked, done, abandoned); its legal values and the legal transitions between them are the one state machine the domain enforces. 'done' and 'abandoned' are terminal.
TaskStatus.lifecycle: New tasks start 'open'. Non-terminal states may move to 'abandoned' directly; other transitions are checked against a table transcribed from the state model. Enforcement lives in exactly one place -- the lifecycle layer's status check and transition table -- never in a caller.

ResolutionItem.definition: One checklist entry (text, done) inside a Task's resolution list. A Task's progress is derived by counting these, never stored as a separate counter.

TaskEdge.definition: A directed, typed connection between two Tasks, with a relation drawn from a fixed, closed vocabulary. Stored separately from Tasks, never inside a Task's own record.

TaskStore.definition: The Repository for Task: reads and writes tasks, edges, and commits. Deliberately does no rule-checking of its own -- validation lives entirely in a separate layer.

ActiveTaskPointer.definition: Which task_id is currently 'active' for a scope -- a single in-memory value, not a stack, and not a field on Task itself.

MemoryRecord.definition: A durable takeaway the loop exists to accumulate -- a constraint, a technique, or a recurring pitfall that Grooming's falsifiable predictions and Introspection's grades produced, and that nothing in Task Tracking can hold. doc 05 and CLAUDE.md call this a 'lesson'; there is no separate Lesson term because there is no separate thing -- a lesson's only persisted form is a MemoryRecord, so the two names would carry identical evidence and identical rules. Its 'standing' (confirmed/contradicted/disputed/superseded) is derived from its confirming and contradicting links to later Tasks, never a value it holds in its own right; its citation to the Task it came from is mandatory, and its 'kind' is a closed vocabulary.

MemoryKind.definition: The kind of a MemoryRecord, drawn from a fixed, closed set of exactly three values (constraint, technique, pitfall). Doc 05 names 'constraint' and 'technique' outright; 'pitfall' earns its place from the accuracy signals, where a recurring 'wrong' or 'missed' grade is a lesson about the loop itself. The set is kept at three deliberately: a longer taxonomy is a decision to make on every capture.
MemoryKind.lifecycle: Set when the MemoryRecord is recorded (defaults to 'constraint') and validated in exactly one place -- the memory record path raises Rejected for any value outside the set. There is no transition machine; re-recording a slug may change its kind.

MemoryRelationship.definition: The label on one link joining a MemoryRecord to a Task, drawn from a fixed, closed set of exactly three values (learned_from, confirmed_by, contradicted_by). 'learned_from' is the mandatory citation every MemoryRecord carries; 'confirmed_by' and 'contradicted_by' are grades a later Task adds. A MemoryRecord's 'standing' is derived from how many confirming and contradicting links it has, never stored.
MemoryRelationship.lifecycle: Written when a MemoryRecord is recorded ('learned_from', implicitly) and when it is linked to a Task (any of the three, idempotently); validated in exactly one place -- the link path raises Rejected for a value outside the set. Links are never updated or deleted except by a forget, which cascades. Standing is recomputed from the surviving links on every read.

Concept.definition: A durable summary of what one source module promises and what must stay true of it -- description, contracts, invariants, evidence. Keyed by module path, enforced 1:1 against the real file tree.

SkillInvocation.definition: A record that a named skill (e.g. commit, task-grooming) ran, optionally against a Task. Deliberately just a lightweight log entry, not a stored, referentially-integral record -- the task reference is not validated. Exists for skill-usage observability only, scoped narrowly so it can't become a second home for decisions or notes.

Methodology.definition: The practice the whole framework exists to make cheap: the four-skill loop -- create, groom, implement, introspect -- together with the docs/methodology/ documents that specify it. It has no artifact of its own, only what each pass writes onto a Task and into Loop Memory. CLAUDE.md calls it 'the asset' and the storage/validation/serving code 'plumbing' subordinate to it: the ontology names every moving part (Grooming, Risk, Introspection, MemoryRecord) but this term names the thing they add up to. Its evidence is the first in this file to cite a docs/ file rather than a taskfw/*.py symbol, because the methodology is embodied in the skills and the methodology docs, not in code.

Grooming.definition: The pre-implementation pass that records a task's current best understanding as falsifiable risks/findings before work starts. Recorded as part of the Task and replaced wholesale each pass -- unlike Introspection, only the latest pass is kept, because grooming is a current-belief snapshot, not a history.

Risk.definition: One falsifiable prediction inside a Grooming pass, and the one part of Grooming that is not wholesale-replaced. A Risk has its own identity and an optional 'graded' verdict that Introspection assigns on whether it held; across re-grooming passes Risks are carried forward and merged by that identity, so a graded Risk -- the loop's primary evidence -- is never silently dropped because a later pass omitted it. Stored as a plain dict inside Grooming, but the shape rule every consumer shares -- coercing a raw entry to that dict and collapsing its text to an identity key -- lives in one place, taskfw/risk.py, rather than being re-derived at each call site.

Introspection.definition: The post-implementation pass that grades how well Grooming's predictions held up and surfaces lessons for Loop Memory. Recorded as part of the Task as an appended series rather than Grooming's replace-in-place snapshot, since each report is evidence about one distinct execution and the series itself is the value.

Implementation.definition: The third pass of the Methodology: doing the work a groomed Task describes, once Grooming has removed enough uncertainty to begin. It is where the plan becomes a change, and where the outcome that Introspection later grades each Risk against is produced. Like Grooming and Introspection it has no artifact of its own, only what it writes onto the Task as it goes: Decisions logged when the choice is made, Commits, and ResolutionItems checked off as they land. Its one intention is to not reintroduce the uncertainty Grooming removed -- staying in scope, and recording reasoning as it happens rather than reconstructing it after.

Nudge.definition: A transient, advisory piece of text attached to the response of an action the caller already took, computed fresh each time. It never blocks the action or changes what gets stored; it only points back at context the caller already has (this task, this memory, this report) and asks it to be looked at again. It exists to keep an omission (nothing worth recording) from ever looking identical to an absence (nothing to record) -- collapsing that distinction into silence is the failure mode a nudge prevents.

TaskContext.definition: The whole pull-based working bundle assembled for one Task in a single call -- task identity, decisions, grooming, graph (parent/children/edges), commits, related tasks, and matching loop-memory lessons, in one fixed section order -- assembled fresh on every call. Two of those sections -- related and lessons -- are approximate (full-text / bm25 matches) and are the first dropped when the bundle exceeds its size budget; every section above them (decisions, grooming, graph, commits) is an exact lookup where a wrong answer would mislead rather than merely disappoint. Exact is not the same as permanent: every section except task identity can still be dropped for budget, and anything dropped is named in the `truncated` field, so a caller can always tell an omission from an absence. This is the concrete mechanism behind 'context is pulled, never pushed' -- nothing about a Task reaches an agent automatically, only through this bundle, and only because the agent asked for it.

Commit.definition: A record that a specific commit (sha, repo) was made against a Task. Stored apart from Task itself, keyed by (task_id, sha), with an idempotent insert -- recording the same sha against the same task twice is a no-op, not an error. Same shape as TaskEdge: never addressed by an id of its own, only reachable through the task it was recorded against.

Event.definition: One entry on a Task's append-only activity log: a timestamped piece of text carrying a kind label from a small closed set. A Decision is one kind of Event; a status change is another. Not a distinct class per kind -- the kind label is the only thing that tells two Events apart -- and the log is never addressed by an id of its own, only read back through the Task it belongs to.

Decision.definition: One kind of Event recorded against a Task: the design-reasoning entry, set down at the moment a real choice was made. What makes an Event a Decision is only its kind label on an otherwise uniform log entry -- there is no separate decisions store to hold it.

GroomingAccuracy.definition: The Methodology's feedback edge read in aggregate: how well a Grooming pass's Risks predicted, gathered across many finished Tasks instead of one. Introspection grades each Risk against a single Task; GroomingAccuracy is what those grades amount to once collected -- the loop's report on itself. Computed from the graded Risks on every read.

GroomingGrade.definition: The verdict Introspection passes on a single predicted Risk, graded against what the Implementation pass actually did: did predicting this help -- did it come true with its mitigation ready, or force the change that avoided it -- or was the pass spent on noise. A label carried on the Risk, the way MemoryKind is a label on a MemoryRecord, absent until Introspection assigns it. A surprise that no Risk predicted is deliberately not a GroomingGrade: with no prediction beneath it there is nothing for a verdict to be about, so it stays part of Introspection's account of what Grooming missed. One GroomingGrade is Introspection closing the Methodology's feedback edge for a single prediction; GroomingAccuracy is what those verdicts amount to across many finished Tasks.
GroomingGrade.lifecycle: Assigned by a single Introspection pass, after Implementation, and carried by its Risk from then on. Re-grooming the same Task keeps the verdict rather than discarding it, so a judgement Introspection has already made is never lost.

Scope.definition: Which project a record belongs to: a scheme-prefixed string derived from the working directory, never typed by hand. `git:<host>/<path>` when a git origin was readable, `path:<abs>` when there was none, `hint:<raw>` when a caller supplied a repo string that could not be resolved to a directory. An attribute, not an entity -- it has no identity of its own, only equality, which is the single operation every consumer needs. The prefix is part of the value because it records HOW the project was known: a fallback must never compare equal to a derived answer, or an omission becomes indistinguishable from an absence. The empty string is a fourth, distinct case meaning 'project unknown' -- carried by every Task written before the field existed, never backfilled, and treated as compatible with every scope rather than as a project of its own.
Scope.lifecycle: Derived once, at record creation, from the workspace in hand, and never recomputed on read -- a record does not change project because someone later read it from somewhere else.

relations.subject: TaskStatus
relations.note: The state field on the Task record. Its closed vocabulary (TASK_STATUSES) and its legal transitions are enforced only in the lifecycle layer, so no caller can validate status differently from another.

relations.subject: ResolutionItem
relations.note: Nested inside task.resolution. Cardinality: zero or more -- resolution defaults to an empty list and nothing enforces a minimum, matching the framework's 'nothing is required' stance.

relations.subject: TaskEdge
relations.note: A TaskEdge only exists in relation to two Tasks; it is never addressed by an id of its own, and removing one is deliberately ungated so a legacy relation type can't get stuck. The parent/child hierarchy is deliberately NOT a TaskEdge -- it is the self-referential Task.parent field, and 'parent_of' was left out of TASK_EDGE_RELATIONS so the hierarchy has exactly one home. Its only rules: an epic Task takes no parent (lifecycle.check_parent), and no Task is its own parent (lifecycle.check_save).

relations.subject: TaskStore
relations.note: The Repository for the Task aggregate; persistence and validation stay separable because TaskStore enforces no rules itself.

relations.subject: ActiveTaskPointer
relations.note: Names the currently-active task_id per scope; never a property stored on Task itself.

relations.subject: MemoryRecord
relations.note: Cited to the task it was learned from -- a pointer into Task Tracking from a different bounded context, never reachable by walking Task's own fields. The citation is one MemoryRelationship row ('learned_from'); see that term for the other two.

relations.subject: MemoryKind
relations.note: The kind label on the MemoryRecord. Closed vocabulary (MEMORY_KINDS) of three values, validated only in the memory record path -- the same single-enforcement-home rule TaskStatus follows.

relations.subject: MemoryRelationship
relations.note: The closed label (MEMORY_RELATIONSHIPS, three values) on each MemoryRecord-to-Task link; those links are what 'MemoryRecord references Task' is built from, and the counts of the 'confirmed_by' / 'contradicted_by' links are what MemoryRecord's derived 'standing' is computed from on every read. Validated only in the memory link path.

relations.subject: Concept
relations.note: SourceModule is deliberately NOT a defined term -- it is a placeholder for 'some file in the repo', declared as the one allowed non-term relation object (NON_TERM_OBJECTS in tests/test_ontology.py) rather than given a definition, because a source file is not a domain noun. Keyed by module path, not by task_id -- Architectural Knowledge shares no term with Task Tracking or Loop Memory; the only connection between the three bounded contexts is this ontology file itself.

relations.subject: SkillInvocation
relations.note: Carries an optional reference, but it is unvalidated and one-directional -- a Task has no field or list that points back to the skills invoked against it.

relations.subject: Methodology
relations.note: One Task is walked through the loop; the Methodology's only footprint is what each pass writes onto the Task (grooming, introspection, decisions, commits) and into Loop Memory (lessons). 'describes' rather than 'part-of' because the practice is the larger thing and the Task is what it operates on -- the Task exists without ever being groomed, the loop does not exist without a Task to run against.

relations.subject: Grooming
relations.note: The falsifiable-claims half of the one feedback edge that separates this from a paperwork ritual (CLAUDE.md: 'Grooming makes falsifiable claims. Introspection grades them.'). Grooming is also 'part-of Task' -- the pass belongs to the Methodology, its recorded output belongs to the Task.

relations.subject: Introspection
relations.note: The grading half of the feedback edge, and the step CLAUDE.md names as the first to rot because skipping it always feels like progress. Like Grooming it is also 'part-of Task': the pass is the Methodology's, the appended report series is the Task's.

relations.subject: Implementation
relations.note: The pass between Grooming and Introspection -- create, groom, implement, introspect -- and the only one that changes the codebase. It owns no store of its own: its outputs are Decisions, Commits, and checked ResolutionItems on the Task, exactly as Grooming's output is the Task's grooming and Introspection's is the report series. Named as its own term so GroomingGrade can be defined as a verdict on what this pass did, rather than leaving 'implement' an unnamed step inside Methodology's definition.

relations.subject: Introspection
relations.note: Introspection grades every Risk against what Implementation actually did; a GroomingGrade is that comparison for one prediction. Before Implementation was a term the feedback edge had a verdict (Introspection), a thing predicted (Risk) and an aggregate (GroomingAccuracy), but no name for the reality the prediction was about.

relations.subject: Grooming
relations.note: Recorded as part of the Task and replaced wholesale each groom pass -- except its Risks, which merge by id (see 'Risk part-of Grooming').

relations.subject: Risk
relations.note: The one exception to Grooming's wholesale-replace rule: risks merge by id across re-groom passes so a graded verdict is never silently lost, while every other Grooming field still replaces in place.

relations.subject: Introspection
relations.note: Recorded as part of the Task; an appended series rather than Grooming's replace-in-place snapshot, reflecting that each pass is a distinct piece of evidence.

relations.subject: MemoryRecord
relations.note: Introspection is where a lesson is surfaced for possible promotion into Loop Memory -- a report carrying a lesson with no cited memory triggers a Nudge, so the omission stays visible instead of silent.

relations.subject: TaskContext
relations.note: One bundle is assembled per task_id on demand and has exactly one Task as its subject -- 'describes' rather than 'references' because that Task is what the whole bundle is about (the neighbour Tasks it also embeds are the separate 'references Task' edge).

relations.subject: TaskContext
relations.note: The bundle's graph section pulls a Task's edges fresh on every call, capped per direction -- edges are read into the bundle, never duplicated into it.

relations.subject: TaskContext
relations.note: The bundle's lessons section is the guaranteed read path back into Loop Memory (see MemoryRecord's Introspection link for the write side) -- without it, a lesson only reached an agent if it happened to look for it directly. Like related, this section is an approximate (bm25) match and among the first trimmed when the bundle is over budget, with any drop reported in `truncated` -- so the exact/approximate split is visible from both approximate sections' relations, not only from 'references Task'.

relations.subject: Nudge
relations.note: A nudge speaks only about the one task or memory the triggering call already touched, never some other record the caller didn't ask about -- it rides on a response, it does not fetch or add a fact of its own.

relations.subject: Nudge
relations.note: One nudge checks whether a just-recorded Introspection report's lessons have been promoted to a MemoryRecord yet, without itself writing to Loop Memory.

relations.subject: Commit
relations.note: A Commit only exists in relation to the task it was recorded against, keyed by (task_id, sha) with an idempotent insert -- same shape as TaskEdge, never addressed by an id of its own.

relations.subject: Decision
relations.note: Logged via the same generic Event path status changes use, distinguished only by its 'decision' kind label.

relations.subject: Decision
relations.note: A Decision is an Event with its kind label set to 'decision'; a status change is the same Event mechanism with a different label. The Decision term and this relation describe that entry from two angles: what a decision-kind Event is for (the Decision term) and that it is one value of a closed kind set on a uniform log (this relation).

relations.subject: Event
relations.note: An Event only exists on one Task's append-only log; it is never addressed by an id of its own, only read back through the Task -- the same shape as TaskEdge and Commit. The closed kind vocabulary is what tells a Decision-kind Event from a status-change Event.

relations.subject: TaskContext
relations.note: The bundle's commits section pulls a Task's recorded commits fresh on every call, matching TaskContext's own definition -- without this relation the definition named a section the ontology did not otherwise back with a term.

relations.subject: TaskContext
relations.note: The bundle's decisions section pulls a Task's decision-kind events fresh on every call, matching TaskContext's own definition -- without this relation the definition named a section the ontology did not otherwise back with a term.

relations.subject: TaskContext
relations.note: Distinct from 'describes': the bundle also embeds full Task summaries beyond the one it was built for, by two unlike paths. Parent and children arrive in the graph section as an exact deterministic traversal (store.get(parent), children WHERE parent=?) -- a wrong answer there would be misleading, not merely unhelpful. Full-text neighbours arrive in the related section as an approximate bm25 match, and related is the first section trimmed when the bundle is over budget. Neither path ever returns the same Task the bundle describes.

relations.subject: GroomingAccuracy
relations.note: The per-Risk 'graded' verdicts across finished tasks are the sole source; the grooming_accuracy tally in an introspection report is recomputed from them every call and only cross-checked, never read back as truth. Same derive-don't-store reason as progress-from-checklist and standing-from-links -- a stored aggregate can drift from its own evidence.

relations.subject: GroomingAccuracy
relations.note: The aggregate form of the one feedback edge (CLAUDE.md: 'Grooming makes falsifiable claims. Introspection grades them.'). Risk carries that edge for a single task; GroomingAccuracy closes it for the loop itself -- repeated 'wrong' grades mean grooming asks the wrong questions, repeated 'missed' grades mean it asks too few, and both are signals to change grooming rather than note the miss.

relations.subject: GroomingGrade
relations.note: The verdict label on a Risk's 'graded' field. Closed vocabulary (GROOMING_GRADES) of three values, absent until Introspection assigns it and merged forward by risk id across re-grooming passes so a graded verdict is never silently lost.

relations.subject: GroomingAccuracy
relations.note: GroomingGrade is the unit GroomingAccuracy counts: its tallies, predictive_value, and the 'wrong'-share signal are all counts of GroomingGrade values across finished Tasks, where the sibling 'references Risk' edge is about which Risks it reads rather than what it tallies. A value outside GROOMING_GRADES is bucketed as 'unrecognised' and still reported, never dropped, so the grade count can never silently disagree with the risks seen.

relations.subject: Scope
relations.note: The project field on the Task record, written once at creation by tasks__create. Empty on every Task predating the field, which reads as 'project unknown' rather than as a project.

relations.subject: Scope
relations.note: task_commits.repo is normalised through the same derivation, so a commit's project and a task's project are the same kind of value and can be compared. This column is where free-text project identity was observed fragmenting into five spellings of two projects.

relations.subject: TaskContext
relations.note: The bundle's two approximate sections read Scope, and diverge on it: `related` excludes a neighbour from another project outright, while `lessons` returns it marked cross_project, because loop memory exists to generalise across projects and hiding a foreign lesson would defeat the subsystem to enforce a boundary it was built to cross.
